Predictive Maintenance in European Mid-Market
Manufacturing
Industry Benchmark Report 2025 - Northfield Research

Executive summary
This report surveys 412 plant managers across Germany, Italy, Poland and the Netherlands.
Adoption of predictive maintenance (PdM) among plants with 250 to 2,000 employees reached 47%
in 2025, up from 18% in 2021. Adopters report a median 23% reduction in unplanned downtime and
a 14% reduction in maintenance spend within 24 months.
Despite this momentum, 53% of plants have not started. The main blockers are unclear return on
investment (58%), legacy PLC equipment that cannot stream data (52%) and poor data quality
(47%). Companies that began with a single pilot line reached payback in a median of 19 months;
those that launched plant-wide programmes took 31 months.

1. Adoption trend

Adoption has grown at roughly 7 points per year since 2021. Germany leads at 58%, followed by
the Netherlands at 51%, Italy at 42% and Poland at 31%. Automotive suppliers and food processors
are the fastest adopters; metal fabrication lags at 33%.
Growth has been driven by falling sensor prices (down 35% since 2021) and by cloud analytics
bundled with equipment service contracts.

2. Barriers to adoption

Unclear ROI is the most cited barrier (58%). Plants that ran a structured business case before the
pilot were 2.4 times more likely to scale beyond the pilot. Skills are a rising concern: 41% lack
in-house data engineers, and only 12% have a reliability engineer who also codes.

3. Economics

A typical five-plant rollout costs EUR 3.4m over three years (sensors 38%, software 27%,
integration 22%, training 13%). Net benefit turns positive in year 1 and reaches EUR 3.1m
cumulative by year 3, driven by avoided downtime (62% of benefit), lower spare parts inventory
(21%) and energy savings (17%).

4. Implementation approaches
Approach

Median payback (months)

Success rate

Single pilot line, then scale

19

71%

Plant-wide launch

31

44%

Vendor-managed service

24

63%

Pilot-first approaches succeed more often because they surface data issues early.
Vendor-managed services trade lower upfront effort for higher long-run cost and lock-in; 38% of
such adopters said they would not renew on current terms.

5. Recommendations
1. Start with one high-downtime line and a written business case. 2. Retrofit gateways to legacy
PLCs rather than replace them; this cuts integration cost by roughly 40%. 3. Hire or train one
reliability engineer per two plants. 4. Review vendor lock-in clauses before signing multi-year
services. 5. Track three KPIs from day one: unplanned downtime hours, maintenance cost per unit,
and mean time between failures.
Methodology: online survey, March to May 2025, 412 respondents, margin of error plus or minus
4.8 points at 95% confidence. Figures for economics are modelled from 37 case studies.
